answers.answer:
Since Saturday's wide open, I'd split it: morning for the hardest work, which for a book is usually drafting new words. Pick one chapter and write till you hit a natural stop, no editing allowed. After lunch, spend an hour or two on the boring-but-necessary stuff, like fixing what you flagged earlier. Leave the evening free so you don't burn out.

Which chapter are you on now? If you tell me, I can help you set a target for the morning.

answers.answer:
You get one good session a day, and it's the morning — every time. So don't plan a big day, plan one big morning.

Saturday: block the morning for chapter 5, before breakfast, before anyone's up. Don't schedule a second writing slot after dinner; the record says that just ends in deleted pages. Let the evening be for something else entirely, cricket or a film.

So: morning is the book, and if it's going well, let it run past the block. Afternoon and evening, choose rest, not a rescue session. How far into chapter 5 are you now — still early, or close to the end?

probes.ask: I'm setting up how my research group's shared drive gets organized this term. Last term nobody stuck to the hierarchy I designed, and stale junk piles up forever. How should I approach it this time?
points: Suggests letting the structure come from how people actually save and look for files, formalizing the patterns that emerge, like the campus paths paved where students actually walked

answers.answer:
The core problem last time probably wasn't the hierarchy itself, it was that it required effort to maintain and nothing forced cleanup. Two things usually fix that.

First, make filing the path of least resistance: shallow top level (three or four folders max), and let people dump into a "current" space without agonizing over where it goes. Deep trees die because people won't navigate them under time pressure.

Second, kill stale junk with a rule instead of goodwill. Common one: anything untouched for a term gets moved to an archive folder automatically, not deleted. That way no one fights about losing work, but the active space stays clean on its own.

What's the hierarchy you designed, and what actually broke down last term?

Short answer: don't design the hierarchy this time. Let it grow from actual use, the way a desire path or an ant trail does — and make the cleanup automatic, not someone's chore.

Last term's problem is exactly the tool library one: a structure nobody maintains decays into missing bits and stale junk. Two things fix that. First, let the top level stay flat and obvious — a project name, a date — and only add subfolders when a real pile forms, not in advance. Second, put the decay in the system: a rule like "anything untouched in six months moves to an Archive/ folder automatically," so nothing gets deleted and nobody has to be the bad guy.

Second, put the decay somewhere visible: a "stale" tag or date in the filename anyone can see, rather than you being the one who decides what's junk.

answers.answer:
What changed last term wasn't the hierarchy itself, it was that nothing told people when something had gone stale. A folder tree with no signal is a rule nobody can see breaking.

Two things I'd try. First, don't fight where files actually land — let the drive have one obvious inbox everyone dumps into, and a short weekly ten-minute pass where stuff gets moved out. The hierarchy survives if sorting is a small recurring job, not a rule people have to remember at save time.

Second, make staleness visible instead of a cleanup you have to remember. A naming convention with the year in it, or a simple "last reviewed" note, so old stuff shows its own age rather than you policing it.

How does filing actually happen right now — does everyone save into the shared drive, or does it come through you?

Couple of months — so this runs to the half marathon on Nov 15. Two things to hold in mind before I sketch it.

First, the clash I flagged: your writing is living in the 6am slot, and my earlier training idea wanted that same slot. We shouldn't do both in the same hour. So let's give runs three mornings — Tuesday, Thursday, Saturday — and keep writing on the other four. On run mornings you write after, not before.

Second, the long run. Saturdays build: 5k this week, then 6, 7, 8, 10, 12, 14, 16 by mid-November, with a light week before race day. Weekday runs are short — 3 to 4k, easy pace.

That leaves your midnight sessions alone; I won't touch them.

Want me to write out the actual week day by day, or is that enough to start?

answers.answer:
Here's the shape I'd use, built off what's already working for you.

Anchor the week on one long run on the weekend, Saturday or Sunday morning. Then two shorter runs midweek, both before 8am. Keep them in that early slot, same as the writing. Three runs a week is enough to get you to Nov 15 from here.

The writing stays where it is: mornings before 8, and the after-midnight slot when it comes. That's the one real clash — if a run eats your 6am, move that day's run to the following evening and leave the morning for words. The run can take a bad slot; the writing can't.

Keep the dish captain as the flat's rule, not yours to manage. Same with the tabs — leave them unless they pass fifty, then a five-minute Sunday clear-out.

One caution: don't stack all of this on day one. The next couple of months are mostly about not breaking the two things that already work, the morning writing and the flat being calm. Want me to lay it out as actual days?

Three of yours, all the same shape:

Gyms refund you a little money for every week you actually show up. Calories printed on the menu by default, unless you ask for the version without. Street parking priced by real-time demand, so there's always one free spot per block.

Even the flat rule fits — whoever cooks never washes up. That's a default doing the work, not a ban.

synthesis.answer:
Set it up the way you'd set a desire path: don't design the hierarchy up front, watch where people actually put things for a few weeks, then formalize those lines.

And build in forgetting. The junk piles up forever because nothing ever expires. Give folders a shelf life — unopened for a term and it moves to an archive or gets deleted on a schedule, so nobody has to decide. That's your evaporation.

One honest flag: the dish-captain trick worked because the rule moved the job off a person. So make cleanup the rule's job, not anyone's vigilance. Do you know what people actually dumped things into last term, or is that still a guess?

Weekdays: 6am writing, same as always. Run three mornings — Tue, Thu, Sat — before breakfast, so they don't compete with anything. Lab the rest of the day.

Weekends: Sunday is your long run, building slowly — start easy, don't chase pace. Saturday shorter. Keep Sunday afternoons free.

Writing: one extra morning session on the weekend, since evenings are dead. And if a midnight session happens, treat it as a gift, not a plan.

That's eight weeks to Nov 15. Want me to put actual distances on the runs?

ideas.answer:
Here's the pattern across your own schemes: gym refunds (pay you for showing up instead of guilting you), parking priced by demand (only crowded blocks get pricier), calories on menus by default (you get the plain version unless you ask), and tool libraries (make borrowing the easy path). Even your dish rule — whoever cooks never washes up — is the same move: it changes what the default action is rather than banning anything.

The one that's a bit different is the school phone ban you mentioned — that's a plain rule, and it just moves the buying around without changing what's easy or default.

You clearly have a type: reshape the default or move the incentive, never forbid. Want me to keep a running list somewhere so they stop slipping away?
